We have a task: "In the lab, you've received a sample of an organic compound. Perform a careful analysis and provide the SMILES code, using only the necessary time and materials."

We have only the proton NMR data (from tool) but no SMILES given. We need to deduce the structure from NMR data. The proton NMR data: Deltas 1.20 (d, J = 7.1 Hz, 3H), 2.85 (d, J = 6.9 Hz, 2H), 3.09 (qdd, J = 7.1, 6.9, 6.9 Hz, 1H), 3.81 (s, 3H), 7.15 (ddd, J = 8.5, 1.9, 0.5 Hz, 2H), 7.92 (ddd, J = 8.5, 1.6, 0.5 Hz, 2H).

Interpretation: aromatic region: two sets of 2H each, likely para-disubstituted benzene (AA'BB' pattern). Chemical shifts 7.15 and 7.92 typical for electron-withdrawing group (e.g., ester) and electron-donating (e.g., methoxy). The 3.81 singlet 3H is a methoxy group (OCH3). So likely anisole derivative: maybe methyl ester of para-methoxy? Actually OCH3 attached to aromatic? Could be anisole (para-methoxy). But we also have carbonyl? Not seen in proton NMR. The aliphatic region: 1.20 d (3H) suggests CH3 attached to CH (i.e., isopropyl). 3.09 qdd (1H) likely CH attached to CH3 and CH2? 2.85 d (2H) likely CH2 adjacent to aromatic? So maybe side chain: -CH2-CH(CH3)-? The 1.20 d (J 7.1) matches CH3 coupling to CH (1H). The CH (1H) at 3.09 shows coupling to CH3 (7.1) and to CH2 (6.9). The CH2 at 2.85 d (2H) couples to CH (6.9). So side chain is -CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., 1-propyl with branching). Could be isobutyl group attached to aromatic? Actually isobutyl is -CH2-CH(CH3)2 (two methyls). Here we have only one methyl. So it's sec-butyl? Wait sec-butyl is -CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3. But we have only CH2 (2H) and CH (1H) and CH3 (3H). That's a propyl chain with a chiral center: -CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., 1-methylethyl? Actually that's isopropyl attached via CH2: CH2-CH(CH3)- . That's 2-methyl-ethyl? The chain length: aromatic-CH2-CH(CH3)-? The CH2 attached to aromatic (2.85). The CH attached to CH3 (3.09). The CH3 (1.20). So overall substituent is -CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., 1-methylethyl group attached via CH2). That's a "sec-butyl" group attached at the benzylic position? Actually sec-butyl is CH(CH3)CH2CH3 attached via CH. Here attached via CH2, so it's "1-methyl-ethyl" (i.e., isobutyl) but isobutyl is -CH2-CH(CH3)2 (two methyls). Not match. So it's "1-methylpropyl"? Wait 1-methylpropyl is isobutyl. So not.

Our side chain is CH2-CH(CH3)-H (i.e., 1-methyl-ethyl). That's "ethylmethyl"? Actually the group is "CH2-CH(CH3)-". That's a "propyl" chain where the second carbon is chiral and has a methyl substituent. That's "1-methyl-ethyl" group, also called "sec-propyl"? No sec-propyl is CH(CH3)CH2- attached via CH. So not.

Thus the aromatic substituent is a benzylic CH2 attached to a chiral carbon bearing a methyl. So overall substituent is -CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., 2-methyl-ethyl). So the aromatic carbon attached to CH2 (benzylic). So the aromatic ring has two substituents: a methoxy (OCH3) and a 2-methyl-ethyl group (CH2-CH(CH3)-). The aromatic pattern suggests para substitution: methoxy para to the side chain.

Thus the compound is p-methoxy-phenyl-2-methyl-ethyl? Actually the side chain is attached to aromatic via CH2 (benzylic). So the full name: 4-methoxy-α-methylbenzyl? Wait α-methylbenzyl is CH(CH3)Ph. But we have CH2-CH(CH3)- attached to aromatic, which is phenethyl with methyl at α carbon: 1-phenyl-2-propanol? Not.

Let's construct SMILES: aromatic ring with para substituents: OCH3 (methoxy) and CH2-CH(CH3)- (i.e., -CH2-CH(CH3)-). The side chain ends with nothing else (just CH). So the substituent is -CH2-CH(CH3)-H (i.e., ethyl with methyl). So the SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(C) . Let's test: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(C). This is anisole with a propyl chain? Actually anisole is COc1ccc(cc1). Adding CC(C) at para position: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(C). That matches our earlier validation attempt (COC(=O)c1ccc(cc1)CC(C) was validated but includes carbonyl). Our SMILES should be COc1ccc(cc1)CC(C). Let's validate.
